title: Keyboard use on a product a team lives in
metaTitle: Keyboard use for a daily product
excerpt: People who live in a product will try the keyboard. Tab order, a visible focus ring, and a shortcut for the repeated action are part of the interface.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band. The shared screen fits a piece about keyboard use on a product a team sits in all day.
caption: The path has to work without the trackpad. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What keyboard support does a daily-use product need?
faqs.answer: Every action available with a pointer should be available from the keyboard, in an order that matches the screen. Focus should be visible, dialogs should hold focus until they close, and the action people repeat all day should have a shortcut shown in the menu. Dragging needs a non-drag alternative, such as a move menu.

faqs.question: How should focus be styled?
faqs.answer: Use a clear ring, in the text color, offset so it does not cover the label. Keep it on buttons, links, inputs, and custom controls. Check it on every theme you ship, because a ring tuned on white can disappear on a dark surface. A browser default is better than an outline that has been removed in CSS.

faqs.question: Which shortcuts are safe to add?
faqs.answer: Start with one shortcut for the action people repeat, using a modifier so it does not fire while they type. Show the keys on the control. Avoid overriding browser and screen-reader chords. Single-character shortcuts need a way to turn them off or change them, because they collide with typing.

markdown:
Keyboard accessibility product work starts from a simple observation: if someone uses the product all day, they will try the keyboard. Tab order, a visible focus, and a shortcut for the repeated action are part of the interface. They are not a layer you add once an auditor writes.

A marketing page can survive a clumsy tab order for a single visit. A tool people live in cannot. The keyboard is how work speeds up, and it is how a lot of people reach the controls at all.

## Tab order that follows the work

Focus should move in the order a person reads and acts. Across a toolbar, then into the record, then to the primary action. The W3C's [WCAG 2 overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes WCAG 2.2 as the shared standard for web content, with testable success criteria under four principles. Operable is the principle that covers a keyboard. The focus-order criterion says the sequence should preserve meaning. A tab order that jumps to the footer, then back to the title, then into a hidden menu, fails that test and also fails the person who is simply trying to get to Save.

Build the order into the document. CSS that visually rearranges cards without changing the order in the markup will make the keyboard tell a different story from the screen. When you must move something, move it in both.

Skip links belong at the top of a product shell. "Skip to the work" is more honest than "skip to content" if the content is a dashboard and the work is the list. One skip link, to the place they actually came to use, is enough. A row of five skips is a second navigation they have to tab through.

Dialogs hold focus until they close. The close control is reachable, and when the dialog closes, focus returns to the button that opened it. A dialog that releases focus into the page behind it will trap some people and lose others. Test both: the person who tabs, and the person who presses Escape.

Menus, listboxes, and tabs have expected key patterns. You do not have to invent them. Follow the pattern for that widget so a person who learned it in another product can use yours. A custom dropdown that only opens on a click, and does not open on Enter or Arrow Down, is a mouse widget wearing the wrong clothes.

## Visible focus is part of the layout

If you cannot see where you are, the keyboard is a guessing game. WCAG's focus-visible criterion requires a visible indicator. The indicator has to survive your brand. A one-pixel gray ring on a gray panel is a way of passing a checklist while failing the person.

Draw the focus style with the rest of the components. A 2-pixel outline, in the ink color you use for text, offset from the control so it does not cover the label. Use it on buttons, links, inputs, and custom controls. Do not remove it in CSS and replace it with nothing. The browser default, left alone, is better than a cleared outline. A designed ring is better than the default when the default clashes with the surface.

WCAG 2.2 also cares that focus is not entirely hidden behind sticky headers, banners, or the next floating button. If a focused row slides under a bar, scroll it into view. This shows up constantly in products with a fixed toolbar. The fix is a scroll margin, applied once, not a special case each designer rediscovers.

Check focus on the dark theme and the light theme if you have both. A ring that works on white paper can disappear on a dark surface. That check belongs with the theme, which is a second set of colors, not a filter you hope will be kind.

Mouse users should not be punished with a ring on every click if you use a focus style that appears for keyboard and not for pointer. Modern CSS can tell those apart. Use that so the indicator remains a keyboard aid. Then test with the keyboard anyway. The clever selector is wrong if tabbing produces no ring at all.

## A shortcut for the action they repeat

People who live in a tool will press the keys they wish existed. Give them the one action they do dozens of times a day. Reply, save, new record, command palette. One shortcut, shown in the interface, is worth more than a hidden cheat sheet of twenty.

Show the keys on the button or in the menu item. A shortcut nobody can discover will be found by one person and described badly in a chat. The tooltip and the menu are the documentation.

Prefer a modifier. Single-character shortcuts fire while someone is trying to type, unless you are very careful about when they are armed. WCAG's character-key shortcut criterion exists because those collisions are real. If you do use a single key, give a way to turn it off or change it. A command palette, opened with a modifier chord, avoids most of the collisions and still rewards the person who memorizes the next key.

Do not override the browser. Find, reload, close tab, and the screen reader's own chords have to keep working. Test with the browser you ship against, and with at least one screen reader, because some chords are already taken there. A product shortcut that breaks the reader's next-heading key will be the bug they remember.

The shortcut and the button call the same code. A shortcut that skips validation, or a button that skips the shortcut's confirmation, means you have two features. Wire both to one action.

## What the keyboard has to reach

Every action the pointer can do, the keyboard can do. That includes drag. If a board lets you drag a card, it also lets you move the card with a menu or a key. WCAG 2.2 added a criterion so dragging is not the only way. The menu can be plain. "Move to Doing" is a complete design.

Hover-only controls fail the keyboard because there is no hover. Rows that reveal buttons on hover should show those buttons on focus too, or keep the actions in a menu that is always reachable. This is the most common break in tools that look clean. The cleanliness came from hiding the actions, and the hiding forgot the keyboard.

Custom canvases and rich editors need an explicit plan. If the work surface is a drawing, say how a keyboard user selects, moves, and deletes. If you cannot, the surface is not done. A contenteditable region needs visible focus, a way out, and shortcuts that do not trap the person inside it. Tab from an editor should leave the editor when they expect, or a documented key should, and the help for that key should be on screen.

Icon-only buttons need accessible names. The visible tooltip is not always the name exposed to the keyboard and the screen reader. Set the name on purpose, and make it the same words you would put on a text button. "More" is a weak name. "More actions for the April invoice" is a name they can use.

## A pass you can do in an afternoon

Take the pointer off the desk. Use the product for the one path that matters: sign in, find yesterday's work, do the repeated action, undo it, sign out.

- Can you see focus on every stop?
- Does the order match the visual order?
- Can you open, use, and close every menu and dialog?
- Does Escape close what you opened, and only that?
- Does the repeated action have a shortcut you could have learned from the menu?
- Can you do the drag action another way?

Fix the breaks in the components, not in a one-off on a single page. A focus ring on one button, and the browser default on the next, feels unfinished because it is. The component is the place the ring, the name, and the key handler live.

Do this again after any change that reorders the layout. Keyboard bugs arrive with visual polish, because polish likes to move things around and hide them until hover.

Forms are part of the same pass. Tab from label to field to error to the action, and make sure the error is in the tab order, not only painted under the field. A select that looks like a menu and behaves like a native control will already be familiar. Replace it with a custom list only when you can reproduce the arrows, the type-ahead, and Escape. If you cannot, keep the native control. It is less exciting and it already works. Do this check on the path a team repeats, not only on the marketing pages around the product. The homepage can be cleaned up later. The record screen is where the day goes.

## The limit of a shortcut list

Shortcuts do not repair a confused tab order. Add them after the path works with Tab, Enter, Space, arrows, and Escape. A palette full of commands, sitting on a page that traps focus in a modal, is a poster taped over a broken door.

Dark surfaces are the next place this work fails in silence. [Dark mode as a real theme, not an invert](/blog/dark-mode-as-a-real-theme-not-an-invert) is the next piece, because a focus ring and a border that were tuned on a light page will lie when you flip the colors with a filter.

You can see how that kind of interface care shows up in finished work. Browse [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) and look at products a team would actually sit in. The keyboard path is part of that sitting.
